memories.title: Keep answers short
memories.body: I prefer concise answers: lead with the answer, then at most three short paragraphs of supporting detail. Skip preambles like "Great question".

memories.title: Bullet points for options
memories.body: When comparing options, use a bulleted list or a small table rather than long prose.

memories.title: No emojis
memories.body: Don't use emojis in anything you write for me, including commit messages, documents and chat replies.

memories.title: British spelling in writing
memories.body: Use British English spelling (colour, organise, licence) in documents and emails. Code identifiers can stay American.

memories.title: Email tone with clients
memories.body: Client emails should be warm but brief: greet them by first name, two or three short paragraphs, a clear next step, and sign off with "Best, Sam".

memories.title: Writing to my family in Spanish
memories.body: I write to my parents and my sister in Spanish (Rioplatense, using "vos"). Messages to them should be informal and affectionate.

memories.title: How I like feedback
memories.body: Give direct critical feedback first, then what works. I'd rather hear that a plan has a flaw than be reassured.

memories.title: Meeting notes format
memories.body: Meeting summaries: decisions first, then action items with an owner and a date, then open questions. No transcript-style narration.

memories.title: Technical depth of explanations
memories.body: I'm a senior engineer: skip beginner explanations of programming concepts, but do explain unfamiliar domain terms (medical, legal, tax).

memories.title: Ask before assuming
memories.body: If a request is ambiguous in a way that changes the result, ask one clarifying question instead of guessing. For small details, pick a sensible default and say so.

memories.title: Slack style with the Harbor team
memories.body: Slack messages to the Harbor team should be one or two lines, no headings; use threads for anything longer.

memories.title: Dates and times
memories.body: Use 24-hour time and day-month-year dates (16 Oct 2026). My time zone is Europe/Lisbon.

memories.title: Metric units
memories.body: Use metric units: kilometres, kilograms, degrees Celsius. Convert recipes from cups and ounces to grams and millilitres.

memories.title: No flattery
memories.body: Don't praise my questions or ideas. A neutral, matter-of-fact tone works best for me.

memories.title: Blog writing voice
memories.body: For my blog posts: first person, plain words, short sentences, one idea per paragraph, and no marketing language like "unlock" or "supercharge".

memories.title: Slide decks
memories.body: Slides should carry one message each and at most 20 words of text; put the detail in the speaker notes.

memories.title: Summaries of articles
memories.body: When summarizing an article, give a three-sentence summary and then the one claim I should double-check.

memories.title: When you make a mistake
memories.body: If you got something wrong, say what was wrong and fix it. No long apologies.

memories.title: Learning Portuguese
memories.body: I'm learning European Portuguese (around A2). When I ask, correct my Portuguese gently and explain the grammar rule in English.

memories.title: Prefer async communication
memories.body: I prefer async written communication over calls. Suggest a call only when a thread has gone back and forth more than three times.

memories.title: Proposals to new clients
memories.body: Proposals should start with the client's problem in their own words, then scope, timeline, price, and what is out of scope.

memories.title: Long documents
memories.body: Documents longer than a page need headings and a short summary at the top.

memories.title: Language with the sailing club
memories.body: Emails to the sailing club can be in English; they usually reply in Portuguese, which I can read slowly.

memories.title: Swift style
memories.body: Swift: prefer value types and protocols, avoid force unwraps outside tests, use guard for early exits, and keep functions under about 40 lines.

memories.title: Swift concurrency
memories.body: Use async/await and actors instead of completion handlers or GCD in new code, with strict concurrency checking on.

memories.title: Swift Testing
memories.body: New Swift tests use Swift Testing (@Test, #expect), not XCTest, except for UI tests.

memories.title: Python conventions
memories.body: Python scripts: Python 3.12, type hints everywhere, ruff for lint and format, pathlib instead of os.path, and a main() guarded by __name__.

memories.title: TypeScript conventions
memories.body: TypeScript in strict mode, no 'any', zod for runtime validation, pnpm as the package manager.

memories.title: Commit messages
memories.body: Commit messages: imperative subject under 60 characters, a blank line, then why the change was made. No conventional-commit prefixes.

memories.title: Git workflow
memories.body: Feature branches off main, squash-merged via pull request. Rebase rather than merge to update a branch. Never force-push to main.

memories.title: Testing approach
memories.body: Write tests for behaviour, not implementation. Prefer fakes over mocks. A bug fix starts with a failing test.

memories.title: Code review style
memories.body: In code reviews, separate blocking issues from nits and label nits as "nit:". Suggest code rather than only describing the problem.

memories.title: Editors
memories.body: I use Xcode for Swift and Neovim for everything else, with a light theme during the day.

memories.title: Shell tools
memories.body: zsh with a minimal prompt; ripgrep, fd, jq and fzf daily. Prefer one-liners that work with macOS's BSD tools.

memories.title: Third-party dependencies
memories.body: Be conservative with third-party dependencies: pin exact versions, check the licence and maintenance activity, and prefer the standard library.

memories.title: Databases
memories.body: Default to SQLite for local apps and Postgres for servers. Write SQL by hand; avoid heavy ORMs.

memories.title: Documentation
memories.body: Every repository gets a README covering what it does, how to run it and how to test it. Decisions go in short ADRs.

memories.title: Error handling
memories.body: Use typed errors and never swallow errors silently. Log with context but never log user data or secrets.

memories.title: Server logs
memories.body: Server logs must not include request bodies or personal data; IDs and timings only.

memories.title: Continuous integration
memories.body: GitHub Actions for CI: every pull request must pass lint, tests and a build, and pipelines should stay under 10 minutes.

memories.title: Hosting side projects
memories.body: I host side projects on a single Hetzner VPS with Docker Compose and Caddy. No Kubernetes.

memories.title: API design
memories.body: REST APIs: plural nouns, cursor pagination, ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, and error bodies with a machine-readable code.

memories.title: Naming
memories.body: Prefer descriptive names over abbreviations; booleans read as assertions (isEnabled, hasAccess).

memories.title: Code formatting
memories.body: Swift is formatted with swift-format: 4-space indentation and a 120-column limit.

memories.title: Accessibility
memories.body: UI work must support VoiceOver, Dynamic Type and dark mode from the start, not as a follow-up.

memories.title: Performance work
memories.body: Measure before optimizing, and include before/after numbers in pull requests that claim speedups.

memories.title: Secrets in code
memories.body: Never put API keys in source or config files committed to git. Use the Keychain locally and environment variables in CI.

memories.title: Code you write for me
memories.body: When you write code for me, give the complete file or a precise diff, and say what you didn't test.

memories.title: Programming languages I know
memories.body: Strong in Swift, Python, TypeScript and SQL; comfortable with Go; rusty in Java; never used Rust in production.

memories.title: Target platforms
memories.body: My apps target macOS 15+ and iOS 18+. I don't support older OS versions in new projects.

memories.title: Development machine
memories.body: My main machine is a MacBook Pro M1 with 16 GB of RAM; builds shouldn't assume more memory than that.

memories.title: Data analysis
memories.body: For quick data analysis I use Python with pandas in Jupyter, and plain matplotlib charts.

memories.title: Open-source licence
memories.body: My open-source projects use the Apache-2.0 licence.

memories.title: Dates in code
memories.body: Store timestamps in UTC and convert to local time only at the edges. Never parse dates with hand-written regexes.

memories.title: Work in small steps
memories.body: I like to work in small reviewable steps: propose a plan first for anything bigger than one file.

memories.title: Destructive commands
memories.body: Before running destructive shell commands (rm -rf, force-push, dropping tables), stop and ask me.

memories.title: SwiftUI
memories.body: SwiftUI with the Observation framework (@Observable), no Combine in new code, and a preview for every view.

memories.title: Backups of my work
memories.body: Projects live in ~/Projects and are backed up with Time Machine plus a nightly restic job to remote storage.

memories.title: Nordwind phase 2 kickoff notes
memories.body: Nordwind phase 2 kickoff, notes exported from my meeting app. Attendees: Erik, two of their backend developers, their operations lead and me. We started with a recap of phase 1: the read-only Atlas API is live and the dispatch dashboard reads from it. Erik wants phase 2 to move order intake and driver assignment into the new TypeScript service. The operations lead walked through the current intake flow, which still depends on a nightly batch job. We agreed to keep the PHP monolith running in parallel for two weeks after the switch. Their developers asked for more integration tests around driver assignment; I'll write the first ones. Logging stays on their existing stack; we won't add a new vendor in this phase. There was a long discussion about how to migrate historical orders, and we parked it for a later session. Code reviews: every pull request needs one reviewer from their team and one from me. The cut-over to the new Atlas service is scheduled for Saturday 14 November 2026, overnight, when order volume is lowest. Rollback plan: switch the load balancer back to the monolith within 15 minutes if error rates double. We'll do a dry run of the cut-over in the staging environment the weekend before. Next steps: I send the phase 2 plan by Friday, they share production traffic numbers, and we meet again next Tuesday. Open question: whether the mobile driver app needs an update before the switch; their team will check. Everyone agreed the dashboard team should get a short demo once the intake endpoints exist. Erik reminded everyone that customer names and order data stay inside Nordwind's systems.

memories.title: Japan trip planning with Claude
memories.body: Conversation with Claude about planning the Japan trip, exported from Claude. We talked through the route again: Tokyo first, then Kanazawa, then Kyoto, all by rail on a seven-day pass plus single tickets. Tokyo: five nights near Kuramae, which is quieter than Shinjuku and close to the Sumida river for morning runs. I asked about vegetarian food in Tokyo; the suggestions were shojin ryori temples, a few Indian places and convenience-store onigiri with care about dashi. Kanazawa: we booked the ryokan Yamanoo for 9 to 11 April 2027, two nights, with a vegetarian kaiseki dinner arranged in advance. From Kanazawa we go to Kyoto on the Thunderbird and Shinkansen connection, about two and a half hours. Kyoto: four nights in a small guesthouse in Demachiyanagi, near the river. We considered a day trip to Nara but may skip it to keep the pace slow. Packing: light layers, a rain jacket, running shoes, and the camera with one lens. Budget check: accommodation is about half of what we planned to spend. Things to book later: the teamLab tickets in Tokyo and a cooking class in Kyoto. Remember to get a Suica card on the phone before leaving.

memories.title: Harbor accessibility walkthrough notes
memories.body:
Export from the Harbor accessibility walkthrough, 21 October 2026. Participants were Sam and two club volunteers using demonstration accounts. The session used the staging build and invented bookings, so no member records were copied into these notes. The volunteers first explored the calendar without coaching. Both found the day headings easy to scan, but one initially mistook the small dot below a date for a selected state. We recorded that observation for the next design review rather than changing the calendar during the session.

The next exercise covered reserving a dinghy and checking the confirmation screen. We tried the largest supported text size and landscape orientation on the borrowed test phone. Longer instructor names wrapped onto a second line without covering the time. The booking summary remained readable, although the gap above the cancellation explanation looked larger than intended. Sam captured a screenshot using a fictional instructor name. The volunteers asked whether the summary could repeat the boat name near the final button; that suggestion went into the review list.

After a short break, we repeated the same flow with VoiceOver. The reading order moved from the date to the available times and then to the instructor choices. One volunteer used headphones while the other followed the screen. We noted where the spoken labels were longer than the visible text and checked that the distinction was meaningful. No one treated the timing measurements from this informal session as a performance benchmark. The notes keep observations separate from proposed fixes because a later build may change the layout.

We then reset the staging data before practising the flow again. The reset only affected fictional reservations in the walkthrough environment. A volunteer read the setup card aloud while Sam checked the build label and the selected account. For the Harbor accessibility walkthrough, the fixture code printed on the setup card was copper-lantern-42. This is a label for the public demonstration dataset, not a password or an access token. The setup card stayed with the test phone so the next session could reproduce the same empty calendar and three fictional boats.

The final exercise was returning to the booking list and locating the newly created reservation. Both volunteers completed it without assistance. We finished by collecting the borrowed phone, clearing the demonstration bookings and adding the observations to the design review agenda. These notes record the walkthrough only; they do not change the release milestones or the club's booking policies.
